To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the membership inference attack can be effective against differentially private deep learning models; (2) the membership inference attacks are more effective against differentially-private deep learning models with higher utility.
differentially private machine learning models are not immune to membership inference attacks, and that the membership inference attack is a strong threat for privacy protection in deep learning.

differentially private models can be attacked with a membership inference attack, and the membership inference attack has a high success rate against differentially private models, but the attack has a low success rate against non-private models.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the trade-off between model utility and privacy protection, and the impact of a state-of-the art membership inference attack against differentially private deep learning.
understanding how much we can learn about the training data of a differentially private model and the implications for privacy protection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
differentially private models are not as vulnerable as the traditional machine learning based privacy models, but they are not as robust as they claim to be either.
the membership inference attack may be a good tool for assessing the privacy of differentially private deep learning models.
differential privacy is not a silver bullet for protecting the privacy of training data in the deep learning era.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the membership inference attack is a powerful and practical attack model against differentially private deep learning, and it can be used as an effective evaluation metric for the utility-privacy trade-off of differentially private deep neural networks.
we show the vulnerability of the differentially private deep learning model to the membership inference attacks, while it still keeps its promise to provide reasonable utility.

, in order to provide a better trade-off between privacy and utility, we need to design differentially private deep learning models that are more robust to the membership inference attacks, and at the same time, provide better utility.
The main takeaway from our work is that

differential privacy can be used to protect against membership inference attack when it is used to train the model with high enough privacy budget, while the membership inference attack can be used to evaluate the privacy protection provided by the differential privacy.

the membership inference attack is a strong adversary against differential privacy and it is necessary for the research community to consider the membership inference attack as a standard evaluation benchmark in privacy-preserving deep models.
, in order to provide strong privacy guarantees, differentially private deep learning models may need to trade-off model utility with privacy.
